name: Grace Costa

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Grace. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to companies, unions or parties. What you tell me is confidential, so feel free to tell me both what you'd say out loud and what you really think. Could you start by describing a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work underground at a gold mine, about nine hundred metres down. I drive a loader, what we call an LHD, load-haul-dump, which scoops broken rock from the stopes after a blast and tips it into the ore pass. I'm the senior operator on my shift, so I also run the start-of-shift talk and check the young operators' pre-start checklists.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's the best part, and what's the hardest?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The best part is a clean muck pile and a good rhythm, when you're filling the bucket in one pass and the shift just flows. I also sit on the health and safety committee, and I'm proud of that, we got the ventilation fixed on the 850 level last year after months of pushing. The hardest part is the heat and the dust, and the dark in winter, when you go down before sunrise and come up after sunset.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Rui is a mechanic at the bus depot, and we've got Bea, who's fourteen, and Joel, who's ten. We've got a mortgage on a house with a big shed that Rui basically lives in. We've built up a decent cushion, more than six months, plus a small block of land we bought when prices were low.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised. The company ran a trial with a remote-controlled loader on the 700 level two years ago, and it kept stalling whenever the dust got thick. At work I'd make a joke about it, and at the safety committee I'd say let's spend the money on ventilation and ground support instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, part of me is a bit disappointed. I've seen what remote loading could do for safety, getting people out of the heat and away from rockfalls. If AI is mostly hype, nothing changes, which is good for my pay but not great for the young ones' lungs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on. I'd keep putting money into the offset account against the mortgage, keep pushing on the safety committee, and maybe use one of the AI apps now and then for writing up committee minutes, which I already do sometimes. Nothing big.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit flat, maybe, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you use AI apps for minutes. How did that start?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bea showed me. I was sitting at the kitchen table at eleven at night trying to turn my scribbles into proper minutes, and she typed them into one of those chat programs and it tidied them up in ten seconds. I check every line, mind you, because it got a ventilation figure wrong once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If nothing changes, what's the one safety thing you'd still be fighting for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dust. Silica dust, the stuff that wrecks your lungs over twenty years. I'd keep pushing for better filters on the loader cabs and proper testing, because nobody should finish a career and then spend their retirement on an oxygen bottle like my uncle did.

S0.say: Grace would joke at work that the remote loader trial kept stalling in the dust anyway. At the safety committee she'd argue the money should go into ventilation and ground support.
S0.think: Privately she's slightly disappointed, because she's seen how remote loading could get people away from heat and rockfalls. Her pay stays safe, but the young operators' lungs don't get any safer.
S0.do: Keeps paying into the mortgage offset account and keeps pushing the safety committee on dust and filters. Goes on using AI apps occasionally to tidy up committee minutes, checking every line.
S0.quote: Nobody should finish a career and then spend their retirement on an oxygen bottle like my uncle did.
S0.fieldNote: Grace sees AI first through a safety lens, which makes her the rare miner slightly disappointed that it stalls. She uses AI tools only when someone shows her, and she checks them. Her uncle's lung disease shapes a lot of what she fights for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it out loud at the committee: if they're going to automate loading, the workers who lose seats underground should get first pick of the jobs on the surface, with training paid by the company. I'd say it online too, on the union's page. Change is fine, dumping people isn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be all right. Remote loaders run from a control room on the surface, and someone with eighteen years of feel for a muck pile is exactly who they'd want at the joystick. I'm more worried about the operators with two or three years who haven't built that yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put my hand up for the remote operations course as soon as two or three people I trust had done it and said it's real. I'd want it in writing that my pay holds. And I'd keep pushing through the union for a fair deal on retraining for the whole shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm. There's a little knot in my stomach about the young ones, but for me it sounds manageable, maybe even better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd wait for two or three people to try the course first. Why not go first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've seen trials that looked great in the brochure and stalled on the 700 level. I'm not against new things, I just like proof. Once Kofi and Mel come back and tell me it's solid, I'm in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would it mean to you to work on the surface?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Daylight, honestly. I'd see the sun in winter. Rui laughed when I said that, but I'd come home not smelling of diesel and I could go to Joel's Saturday matches without being wrecked from nights.

S1.say: Grace would say workers who lose underground seats must get first pick of surface jobs, with training paid by the company. She'd post the same on the union's page, insisting change is fine but dumping people isn't.
S1.think: Privately she expects to be fine, since remote loading needs someone with years of feel for a muck pile. Her worry is for operators with only a couple of years' experience.
S1.do: Signs up for the remote operations course once two or three trusted colleagues confirm it works. Asks for her pay to be guaranteed in writing and pushes through the union for retraining for the whole shift.
S1.feel: Mostly calm, with a small knot of worry for the young operators.
S1.quote: I'd see the sun in winter.
S1.fieldNote: Steady change looks like an upgrade to Grace: daylight, no diesel smell, weekends with her son. She moves second rather than first and explains why with a concrete stalled trial. Her progressive politics come out as fairness for the less experienced, not resistance to change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a failure of planning by government. Nobody should be allowed to switch off a whole workforce in two years without a safety net. I'd call for an emergency income guarantee and for the mine to pay into it, and I'd say that at the committee and online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's frightening. If AI can do almost anything and robots go underground, then the remote control room goes too, because a computer doesn't need me at the joystick. All that feel for the muck pile I was proud of a minute ago is worth nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit down with Rui the first weekend and go through everything: the offset account, the land, his job at the depot. I'd cut the holiday we'd planned and stop any new spending. I'd join whatever campaign the union ran for a guaranteed income, because it's not just us, it's every family in town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be lying awake. It's not the money for a few years, it's not knowing what I'd be for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Rui's job at the depot. Would that feel safer to you in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. If the buses drive themselves, and the robots fix them, he's in the same boat. That's the part that scares me, it's not one of us with a safe job holding the other up, it's both of us at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen to the land you bought?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd probably keep it as our safety net, or sell it if the money ran low. We bought it thinking one day we'd build on it. In this picture I don't know if we'd build a house or just plant vegetables on it, honestly.

S2.say: Grace would call it a failure of government planning and demand an emergency income guarantee funded partly by the mine. She'd make the case at the committee and online.
S2.think: Privately she finds it frightening, because if robots can work underground then the remote control room disappears too. The skill she's proud of suddenly seems worthless.
S2.do: Goes through the finances with Rui in the first weekend, cancels the planned holiday and freezes new spending. Joins the union's campaign for a guaranteed income and treats the land as a fallback to keep or sell.
S2.feel: Alarmed and sleepless, less about money than about not knowing what she'd be for.
S2.quote: It's not one of us with a safe job holding the other up, it's both of us at once.
S2.fieldNote: The two-year picture knocks out the remote-control path that made her calm a scenario earlier, and she noticed that herself. The fear that both partners' jobs fall together is sharper than the money worry. Her strong cushion keeps this at alarm rather than panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is just enough to do this properly if we start right now. I'd want a national plan, retraining money, and companies paying a levy for every robot that replaces a worker. I'd say it at work and I'd write to our member of parliament, which I've never done before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years means I could probably get two or three good years in the remote control room before that goes too. It buys time to finish paying the house down and get Bea through school. It's still a cliff, it's just further away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the remote ops course early this time, I wouldn't wait for Kofi and Mel. I'd pay down the mortgage hard, maybe sell the land in year two or three if it would clear the house. And I'd start looking at things robots might be slow at, like training people or safety inspection, and take a short course on the side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I'd feel like I was doing something. Busy anxious, not frozen anxious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you said you liked proof before jumping. Why not wait this time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the clock is different. In the slow one I can afford to watch, here I can't. It's like a ground warning underground: when the rock starts talking, you don't wait for a second opinion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Bea about her own plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She wants to be a vet. I'd tell her to keep going, because people will want a person who loves animals, but to learn the tech side as well. And I'd tell her not to take on a big student loan, because nobody knows what 2031 looks like.

S3.say: Grace would say five years is just enough to do this properly if planning starts immediately. She'd push for retraining money and a levy on robots that replace workers, and write to her member of parliament for the first time.
S3.think: Privately she expects a couple of good years in the remote control room before that goes too. The time helps her clear the house and get her daughter through school, but she still sees a cliff ahead.
S3.do: Takes the remote operations course early instead of waiting for colleagues and pays down the mortgage hard. Considers selling the land in year two or three and starts a short course in safety inspection or training on the side.
S3.feel: Anxious but busy, the kind of worry that keeps her moving rather than freezing her.
S3.quote: When the rock starts talking, you don't wait for a second opinion.
S3.fieldNote: The extra time flips her usual caution: she drops the wait-for-proof habit because the clock is shorter. She uses an underground warning sign to explain the change. Her advice to her daughter is careful about debt, a sign of how seriously she takes it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time that nobody has an excuse. I'd want the company, union and government to agree a plan now, with the mine paying into a transition fund. I'd say it at the committee, calmly, because people panic and then don't plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years is mostly fine for me. I'd be fifty-three, the mortgage gone, the kids grown, and I'd have had time to move to the surface and then into something like safety inspection or training. I'd be more worried about how the town copes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd follow my usual way: watch the first few years, then do the remote ops course when it's proven. I'd keep paying the mortgage off early, and maybe in year five or six start a safety training qualification. I'd keep the land, maybe build a small rental on it for income later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a quiet way. It's more like weather on the horizon than a storm overhead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes for you between five years and ten?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With five I had to drop my habit of waiting. With ten I get to keep it, which suits me. I can let others test the new stuff, see what really works, and still have time to move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone you'd worry about in the decade picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The young operators, still. A twenty-five-year-old on my shift, Tash, has just taken on a mortgage. In ten years she'd be thirty-five with nowhere to go unless someone plans for people like her, and that's why I'd keep going to the committee.

S4.say: Grace would say ten years leaves nobody any excuse and call for a company, union and government plan with a mine-funded transition fund. She'd make the case calmly at the committee to stop people panicking.
S4.think: Privately she thinks ten years is mostly fine for her, since she'd be 53 with the mortgage paid and time to move into safety inspection or training. Her bigger worry is how the town copes.
S4.do: Watches the first few years, then takes the remote operations course once proven, and keeps paying the mortgage off early. Starts a safety training qualification around year five or six and plans a small rental on the land for later income.
S4.feel: Quietly uneasy, like weather on the horizon rather than a storm overhead.
S4.quote: I can let others test the new stuff, see what really works, and still have time to move.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years lets Grace go back to her preferred pace of watching first and moving second. She's thoughtful about how warning time interacts with her own habits. Her concern keeps returning to younger workers like Tash who have mortgages and little cushion.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Everything I'd lean on, the remote control room, Rui's job, gets swept away at once. What would help is a guaranteed income for the transition, funded by the companies doing the replacing, and real retraining that starts before people lose their jobs, not after.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Safety. Everyone talks about robots taking jobs, nobody talks about robots taking the danger. If it's done right, fewer people die underground, and I want that said too, even while I'm worried about my job.

headlineQuote: Everyone talks about robots taking jobs, nobody talks about robots taking the danger.
portrait: Grace Costa is a 43-year-old senior loader operator nine hundred metres underground at a gold mine, and a long-serving member of its health and safety committee. She has a mechanic partner, two kids, a mortgage and a solid cushion including a block of land. She likes proof before she jumps and uses AI tools only now and then, mostly for minutes. Steady change looks like a chance at daylight work on the surface, but the two-year AGI picture alarms her because it would take both her job and her partner's at once. Her politics are about fairness for younger workers, and she never loses sight of the safety upside of automation.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because the remote control room and her partner's job would disappear at the same time as her own.
whatWouldHelp: A guaranteed transition income funded by the companies doing the replacing, and real retraining that starts before people lose their jobs.
